Dear statnet team,

 

I have a question about the implementation of erg models.

I'm trying to fit a erg model on a very large social network dataset,
containing 80 different schools in Belgium. It has about 15.000 respondents.
In particular I'm looking for ethnical and gender homophily , and structural
homophily (class, school and education type).

 

( model2 <- ergm(vlo13 ~ edges + transitive + nodematch("class") +
nodematch("ethnicity") + nodematch("EducType") + nodematch("gender"),
verbose = TRUE) )

dataset by school? I would than look for a model that fits all the 80
networks, and perform a meta analysis to check whether the model has a good
fit for all the different school networks.

So I would split the dataset because:

-          I have to deal with smaller datasets, so it takes less longer to
do the calculations. This makes experimenting with the model much easier. 

-          It is structural impossible to have a relationship with someone
from a different school (because of the geometric distance), so there would
be very large homophily for the variable 'school' when I would do my
analysis on the whole network.

-          There is no theoretical issue when I split the network up by
school, because of this structural restraint. 

 

I hope you understand my question.

Hi Jef,

When one has data on multiple settings in which it is impossible for 
people to nominate those in other settings, then I would strongly 
recommend modeling them as separately.  Otherwise one is confounding two 
different processes.

> be very large homophily for the variable 'school' when I would do my
> analysis on the whole network.

Yes, in this case the MLE for a school-homophily parameter would be 
positive infinity. We know this without having to actually model it 
directly, and doing so won't tell you anything in addition.

Jef, I will forward you a manuscript in which we analyzed multiple schools 
independently, so you can get a sense for how we did it.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] A question about ERGMs and simulating networks with an arbitrary number of nodes
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] A question about ERGMs and simulating networks with an arbitrary number of nodes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hannu.  The answer to your question is yes, it is possible (and  
very easy, in fact, using ergm) to do exactly what you're suggesting:

initialfit <- ergm(network ~ edges + <otherterms>)
parameterestimates <- initialfit$coef
simulate(newnetwork ~ edges + <otherterms>, theta0=parameterestimates)

However, doing this is perilous.  The reason it's perilous is that it  
is not clear that doing the above gives you "statistically similar"  
results.  In fact, it's rather clear that in many cases it does not.

Consider the simplest of all ergms:  The "edges" ergm, where the only  
statistic is the number of edges.  This gives the well-known Erdos- 
Renyi graph model in which each edge has the same probability of  
forming, independent of all others.  If you fit this ergm on a network  
with n nodes, you will obtain as a parameter estimate exactly the  
following quantity:
   log(p) - log(1-p),
where p equals the density of the network, i.e., the proportion of the  
n-choose-2 pairs of nodes that share an edge in your n-node  
(undirected) network.  If you now simulate a new network on m nodes  
with the same ergm and the same parameter estimate, you will recreate  
the same density in your new network, on average.  However, note that  
this does NOT give you the same number of edges on average.  For  
instance, if m = 2n, then the same proportion will produce on average  
more than four times as many edges (because m-choose-2 is a bit more  
than 4 times n-choose-2 when m=2n).  So it is necessary here to be  
very clear about what you mean by "statistically similar".  If you  
mean that you want the same number of edges on average, then you  
cannot merely use the same parameter value obtained using an "edges"  
model.  Perhaps it's more realistic to define "statistically similar"  
in this case to mean "same mean degree", but even in this case the  
"edges" parameter must be adjusted when the number of nodes changes.   
Then again, if "statistically similar" means that you want the same  
network density on average, then it's fine to use the same "edges"  
parameter for different-sized networks.

Now consider using the "density" term instead of "edges" in an ergm.   
The density term equals edges divided by n-choose-2, so it is  
equivalent to the edges term AS LONG AS n REMAINS FIXED, since in this  
case density is simply a constant multiple of edges.  In other words,  
using density alone gives you an Erdos-Renyi graph just as using edges  
alone does.  But if you intend to change the size of the network while  
keeping the network "statistically similar", then once again it is  
necessary to be very specific about defining "statistically similar".   
In particular, using the same parameter value in a new m-node network  
will not give the same density on average (remember, it's the *edges*  
parameter that does this).

If the story is so complicated for even the simplest of ergms, imagine  
what happens for more complicated ones!

I hope this helps.
Dave

messages.body_plain:
Dear Phill,

I was looking around for solutions for your problem a few months ago and 
have found no satisfactory solution, at least not for the problem of 
your size.

For my problem, which was only about 90 by 260 matrix, I then used my 
package for blockmodeling (with sum of squres approach and complete 
blocs, which run the fastest) , which is available at 
http://www2.arnes.si/~aziber4/blockmodeling, but I doubt it will be of 
use to you, as it would simply take to long, if nothing else goes wrong.

When I was looking at the literature, the 2-mode clustering algorithms 
seemed promising (for review see Van Mechelen, Bock and De Boeck, 2004), 
but none of those or similar algorithms seem to be implemented in R. I 
would be very happy if somebody pointed something out.

So my suggestion for now would be that you do cluster separately each 
mode (as when analyzing classical, non network data) and then form 
two-mode blockmodel from that. If you find some at lest reasonably fast 
algorithm, you can try it to optimize this solution.

Best regards,
Ales Ziberna

Iven Van Mechelen, Hans-Hermann Bock and Paul De Boeck (2004): Two-mode 
clustering methods: astructuredoverview. Stat Methods Med Res 2004; 13;

netlogit will do it, but the computations for the QAP replications are 
very expensive; you should expect it to take quite a while.  One can run 
such an analysis in ergm, but the tests it gives you will be essentially 
the equivalent of the classical test option in netlogit (which will be 
faster, but will not help in the case of autocorrelation).  Another 
option is netperm (an optional package within statnet), which fits the 
network permutation models from my 2007 Sociological Methodology paper. 
  I've never tried fitting anything that large using netperm, but it 
will probably be faster than a logistic QAP (though you may need to 
tweak the parameters to get good performance).

Hope that helps,

-Carter

Sorry for the delay...

For me, it was a question of memory handling (RAM and swap). Because, 
when you have to estimate a Curved exponantial family model, memory is 
very soon a problem.

My questionning was: what is the max memory handled by the OS per 
process. Because if your OS cannot handle more than 2.5Gb per process, R 
won't be able to pass this limit.

Debian (and Linux in general) are known to be more efficients with 
memory handling than The OS of Microsoft (windows server entreprise or 
more expensive could also be ok).

If you have to handle a lot of memory, a good idea is to install a Linux 
64bit version or the Debian bigmem kernel. The memory is better handled 
by the OS with this 2 solutions.

Victorin Luisier

Hi Jeff,

Thanks for the code. We have rerun it and note that the error message:
 
 Error in svd(H) : infinite or missing values in 'x'

is just a warning and does not indicate a serious problem. Specifically it
notes that the covariance matrix of the MCMC component of the s.e. is not
positive definite. The net effect is usually that the MCMC s.e. for one or
more coefficients is NA. The code directly deals with it and the estimates
are not unduly effected that is, you can believe the results in the summary
tables, etc.

We should probably make this warning appear only if verbose=T in the next
version.

Thanks for pointing it out.

Mark
